overall_summary: Space-themed content focusing on extreme planetary anomalies and bizarre cosmic phenomena significantly outperforms psychology and animal facts. The channel's top-performing video is 'The Planet of Burning Ice Will Break Your Brain!' with 1,053 views, indicating a strong audience appetite for mind-bending astronomical anomalies that challenge common sense.

winning_patterns.pattern: Extreme Planetary Anomalies & Sensory Space Facts
winning_patterns.evidence: 'The Planet of Burning Ice' (1,053 views), 'The Largest Ocean in Space' (460 views), and 'What Does Outer Space Actually Smell Like?' (368 views) represent the highest tier of performance.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on space topics that feature extreme physics, using high-contrast imagery and sensory-focused hooks (smell, taste, temperature paradoxes).

winning_patterns.evidence: 'Sharks Are Older Than Trees?' reached 302 views, showing that simple, high-contrast comparative facts perform well.
winning_patterns.action: Create more 'X is older than Y' or 'X is larger than Y' comparison shorts using highly familiar subjects.

weak_patterns.evidence: 'Your Brain Is Hiding This From You' (38 views), 'The Real Reason Songs Get Stuck In Your Head' (17 views), and 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' (5 views) consistently underperform.
weak_patterns.action: Pivot away from abstract neurological concepts unless they can be framed with a highly visual, high-stakes external mystery.

next_video.concept: The planet with metal clouds that acts as a giant cosmic mirror.
next_video.opening_direction: Start with: 'Astronomers found a planet that shouldn't exist because it acts like a giant disco ball...'
next_video.twist_direction: Reveal that the planet's clouds are made of titanium and silicate, meaning it literally rains liquid metal.
next_video.reason: Aligns with the highly successful 'Planet of Burning Ice' (1,053 views, posted at 12:44 PM) by utilizing extreme planetary physics, sensory-rich descriptions, and a short, high-retention 15-second format.

experiment: Test a 'Cosmic Scale Comparison' series (e.g., comparing the size of the largest known black hole to our solar system) to leverage the high-performing space affinity while introducing a highly visual zoom-out format.
